💻 After 3+ years building in AI something, I've had the most frustrating 3-4 weeks building and I couldn't really name why. It's finally clicked. For years, I've been designing everything with context as the bottleneck. Now it's something else. ⤵️

Legibility.

And true to the topic, the point I'm trying to back is still a little fuzzy to me, but I'm going to try.

I think when you first start building, you segment projects a lot. You're not building a system, you're building a workflows. Self contained, I add input X, I get output Y, --- and if you're feeling frisky --- it repeats every Z days.

That's where a lot of people stop, and honestly, it might be the right place to stop. But I like systems. I want everything to be connected. I want intake contracts that accept a wide variety of inputs. I want frontmatter schema that determine a wide variety of outputs. I want friction to be a thing to eliminate, not repeat over and over.

So then there's rules. Scripts. Scopes. Fences. Validation checks on everything.

And then it got better and better and better

and then... 

Everything suddenly sucks. Suddenly I'm spending 90% of the time trying to diagnose which of my vErY cLeVeR design decisions are ruining everything.

... and then I just open up a new folder. don't even name it. don't git init. Don't add it to obsidian. Don't prepare a 6-page build spec. 

I just spend 30 mins braindumping a problem. And let it run for 2 hours.

And it works... not perfect... but works.

I'm not going to just switch to rawdogging empty directories. But I did get reminded of how nice everything is before you make it complicated.

My new focus is how to bring feeling into a much more mature system. and I think I have a way to get the best of both worlds.

Tinkering now. Will tell you how it goes.

🚨⚠️ 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗼 𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 is changing rapidly, and is gaining a lot of legal pushback. Here's ⤵️ (non lawyer) 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝘀. ⚠️🚨 

TL:DR: a lot of standard business practice of how videocalls are recorded and transcribed in the EU never met GDPR regulations. But, it was a low concern because a.) people didn't understand, b.) regulators have limited capacity, and this isn't top priority. AI is making it so regulations across the board can be enforced more easily AND an industry is being formed to capitalize on that -- quick and easy legal filings that incentivize people to file as many suits as possible for financial gain. Fun!

Relevant factors to research or get legal counsel on:

𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗘𝗥
🔹 GenAI has lowered the threshhold of the time and skill needed to file a legal complaint. There's an entire industry building on this knowledge arbitrage
🔹 If you're having a video call, this still falls under GDPR. Names, personal details, etc. By recording the call, even transparently your company -- and as a freelancer YOU -- are usually the data controller for that infromation. (consult a lawyer, I'm not 100%)
🔹 Czech Republic has a 1-party consent recording policy for other circumastances, but it doesn't apply to the business use case.
🔹  If you ask to record BEFORE recording, like a normal person, you don't have their permission on the recording itself. Ask for their permission again at the start of the recording to make sure that's on record. (not a lawyer:) I'm also pretty sure their verbal consent even cover the GDPR requirements
🔹 If you use a notetaking bot, do not assume that it's visible presence counts as consent. Do not assume that the others on the chat know what that bot is (or even noticed it)
🔹 The violation is at the time of recording/transcribing. Scrubbing PII out of the calls post-hoc doesn't help.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁. It, and the industry built around it, will build a profit engine around pursuing legal action even if you use it in completely good faith. 

𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗘𝗟𝗦𝗘

🔸 You should know that recording calls and/or transcription is now (and problably has been for a while) completely silent, depending on the tool. Just because you don't see a "Recording" light on, or see a notetaking app in the video call, does not mean you're not being recorded.
🔸 ^ This is not just for people to be sneaky. It's extermely convenient and is easily connectable to AI pipelines. 
🔸 Your voice can now be replicated using AI at 2-5 hours of your captured voice. Less needed by the day, and the range affects the quality not the possibility.

Also, please, I'm begging you, do not, under any circumstances, put images of your children online. If you don't know why, DM me. Won't pitch you, but you need to know.

While not perfect, we're in a local, if not global, maximum of your access to uncensored, (>> relatively! <<) non-manipulated information. Use this time wisely.

There's this idea that the propaganda was a cold war thing, that's declined since (cr-a-zy opinion -- but, real). And then that the internet basically made all information available to those that "do the research"

The logical fallacy is that because there's so much information available to you, that the truth is included in there, and it's just a problem of finding the right "news" that will give it to you.

[Research keywords: Closed-world assumption, WYSIATI, (one step down the ladder: Streetlight fallacy) ]

Remember that slogan they taught you when they were still teaching kids how to read, "knowledge is power?" Well it is. And if you were lucky enough to be part of the generation that DID learn how to read, you can spend 10 mins reading about whether people with power tend to give it away.

[Research keywords... US literacy rates in adults, and then, sadly, for current students; The Machiavellians (Burnham); Iron Law of Oligarchy (Michels).]

Important: people think open weight models are gated behind a $10-20k computer. They aren't. You can rent 100+ VRAM GPUs for like $2-4 an hour. (I recommend RunPod -- not an ad/affiliate)

I cannot say this loud enough:: having open weight models will be viewed the same as keeping a nuclear weapon in you basement in 2, 5, 10? years from now.

The gate is curiosity + 2-20 hours of study to increase your technical competence.

Be curious.

I use LinkedIn in a MANY ways that I'd never recommend to a client. Here's why it doesn't matter (for my business!), but why you probably shouldn't do it for your business. Let's talk inbound vs outbound marketing.

99% of the time when people say marketing, they mean inbound marketing (organic reach + performance).

And yes, I mean digital marketing, because this is 2026. If you want to be pedantic (and or larp as a time traveler), then make sure you correctly say "cellular phone" and "online video game".

But outbound marketing is a thing. Is it a thing people like? Generally, no. But it's a thing.

(as a quick aside, a message that you can complely ignore being disliked MORE than the Human Prompt Injection version is very confusing to me, but that's another post)

Outbound and Inbound, as their names might suggest, have a push / pull dynamic. Which means that the content that supports them has a different function, and on LinkedIn typically don't even have the same viewing interface.

I don't need this post to show up on your feed. I don't need you to share it. I don't need you to like or comment on it. Those are bonuses that ADD a small amount of inbound traffic to my outbound, but make up less than 1-2%.

I need it to do a very simple thing: when I message you on LinkedIn, and you view my profile, I need you to see that I work with AI all day, and at a level that is beyond what you're doing in house. That's it. Try it, scroll through my posts. No really, close this post and scroll through them. Or choose to not learn something new. Your choice :)

I'd add some extra nuance to why my situation is even more specfic and why the expected "wouldn't you rather have both?" question doesn't apply to me. But I'd rather leave it open so that maybe I get a comment or two to get some of that sweet, sweet 1-2%

Claude now seems to default much more to building out python scripts instead of md skills. Probably affects us non-devs more who never even had python installed 6 months ago. 🫠 Here's how I'm (kinda) coping 🔽

I have two interaction surfaces with claude. Terminal and obsidian. Anything that doesn't show up in obsidian, is basically invisible to me.

(for those just tuning in, that's bad)

Oh, and I also have never written a line of python in my life and I don't even know if double clicking a .py script would just execute it or let me read it.

(for those considering hiring me ... look ... I ... ok ... I have other strengths ok?)

>> Here's what I'm doing <<

I have a system primitive called Operator Lens. It's an md file --  ✅ visible in obsidian! -- that corresponds 1:1 with any script (py, ps1, sh, etc) in the system.

It lists (partially in frontmatter, partially in prose):
🔸 what is does -- in plain english
🔸 status -- is it currently active or disabled.
🔸 it's type -- e.g. tooluse hook
🔸 it's scope -- when/where it fires
🔸 key variables I can adjust -- e.g. every X days; from Y dir
🔸 when it was created, and the reason why
🔸 what would be true for it to be working as intended
🔸 what would be true for it to be deleted asap
🔸 log of last 10 times it was fired, and in what context -- i don't have this for tooluse hooks that fire often

Where they live is in flux. I've tried having them be in the same dir that the script itself lives in (basically making the script "visible" in obsidian). But I decided this is probably one of those decisions that come from being a non-dev.

Now I have an indexed folder of Operator Lenses for each working directory that I launch Claude into. 0_ prefix for disabled 1_ prefix for active. (considering a prefix for just active ones, because I'd like them to be sorted to top, but alas)

I guess I have the ability to specify that I want claude to go back to its more skill-based build outs. But I guess I'm stuck in the belief that it's going in that direction for a reason and I should adapt.

But, man, script-based silent failures suuuuuuuck. 

And also, as they become more common, A LOT of people are going to find out that it asks you "do you trust this folder" when you first launch a session into it.

Like for real, I don't think claude checks at all what a script contains before running it ... which is ... problematic.

Sessions and agents/subagents in Claude have changed drastically, and even for someone using claude all day every day it's quite difficult to comprehend all the implications. Here's what I've pieced together so far🔽

Agent view / fleet view (accessed by pressing <- in the CLI) is not just a UI change like I assumed. I used to run multiple sessions in multiple tabs in powershell, and assumed that agent view was simply a way to more cleanly substitute that working style with a more convenient top level display.

This does not seem to be the case.

First of all, sessions now can be enabled to send each other prompts directly. I mistook this as sessions spawning subagents with instructions as has been the case for a long time.

But, no, agents without a parent-child relationship can now send each other prompts. First off, this is huge. And it's obviously an effort to enable the agent-to-agent interaction that seems to be next major step change into how ai permeates across the economy.

All those 'agent swarm attacks' -- that despite mea culpas, seems to be an intended success rather than an accidental mistake -- was probably unlocked  via this new ability.

And even when launching session IN DIFFERENT CWDs!! there is no longer any barrier between them. I see subagents from one working directory in the session from another directory, and peculiar things happen like when asking a session to halt the subagents, it says "these are not my subagents to stop, they come from another session" ---- what??

I thought I was pretty up to date on the relationship between sessions, because ever since the threat of the June 15th "separate but equal 😅" billing between "interactive" and "programmatic" sessions, I've been building my workflows around launching sessions from other sessions using powershell, which means I had to wade through all of the implications of that, meaning understand which env vars get passed along in the process, the primary one relavent to this discussion is the "is child session." (if left to default it would be set as true and the new session would be a child session which has implications on things like whether JSONL transcripts get stored.

All that to say, the changes to these relationships are very different now in ways I don't fully understand and the lack of understanding is breaking a lot of my workflows 😅

What I'm gathering is that it's not just sessions and subagents anymore. Even without "pseudo-interactive" sessions being launched via CLI, sessions seem to be launching actual other sessions, not just subagents. 

This is rambling, sorry, but it's a very big change with big implications. And the fact that all of this is outside of their training cutoff of June means that they also don't understand the changes, and even if you force them to consult anthropic docs, they STILL don't understand these changes. Causing massive confusion and weird behavior on both sides.

TL;DR someone broke my workflow and it's frustrating lol

TL;DR -- Fable is a useful tool for your ai toolkit. But the bottleneck for 99.9% of people isn't the model. it's you 😀

🧠 You were never bottlenecked by thinking. You were bottlenecked by doing.

Agents just broke the chain -- you can finally think first. 🔓

Split any real work into two parts: thinking and doing.

For one person, you could never fully separate them. You can't think for 29 days and execute on the 30th -- the doing takes longer than that. So you oscillate. Think a little, do a little, think, do. Always half in each.

Companies bought their way around it with bodies. In IT we didn't sell hours, we sold mandays -- fan the doing across more people, compress the calendar. Those people were, in hindsight, pre-agents.

But humans are expensive to coordinate. Not just wages -- the rush, the sync, the management overhead all climb the harder you push.

Agents don't work that way. Token spend is token spend. You can plan for 29 days, then fan the doing across as many of them as the work needs, in a fraction of the time.

So the old rule -- execute before you've finished thinking -- is gone.

Think the whole thing through. THEN move. 🚀

What would you build differently if doing was no longer the constraint?

🧠 The bottleneck for ai adoption was never the technology.

It's the people -- and that won't change for 15 years. ⏳

I've spent two years at the commercial edge of this stuff. The tools are already good enough -- you could freeze them today and still get agency-quality work out of them.

So why do most companies stall?

Because someone still has to get real people to actually use it. And that's the part you can't automate. The folks who think AI will run a company in three years have never tried rolling it out in a European org.

Here's the pattern I've watched fail, every time: buy the tool, run one workshop, wait for the adoption that never comes.

What works is slower, and more human. You bring people along -- one reluctant person at a time -- until the tool stops feeling like a threat and starts being a habit.

The companies that win the next decade won't have the best ai.

They'll have the most literate people. 🌱

Where's your team actually at?

right, gently correct anything I missed, and re-explain only the part I
got wrong.

Then close the session with exactly this message to me, in your own
words but preserving the meaning:

"Nice work. The natural next topic that builds on this one is
*anchoring* — the simple habit of periodically re-stating the goal so
the model stays locked on. If you'd like a custom follow-up lesson on
